transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because things have been just so strange at work lately, and it's really starting to become a lot to deal with. I'm a nursing assistant, you see, and I've been doing this for a long time, so I know exactly what the floor is supposed to sound like. I know every beep, every alarm, every little hum of the machines. But lately... well, I keep hearing these voices. 

And I don't mean just murmurs or people talking down the hall, I mean clear as day, exactly like somebody is standing right next to me. They come right out of the call-light speaker at the nurses' station, and even from the HVAC vents in the hallways! At first, I thought someone was messing with the intercom, because the voices are telling me very specific things. They keep telling me exactly which patient records have been changed. The voice from the vent will just start listing off whose charts were altered and what was hidden in them. 

And the most frustrating part about all of this is that it happens even when the unit is completely quiet. It can be dead silent on the floor, and I'll hear it so loudly and clearly, but nobody else hears it! None of the other nurses or techs hear a single thing. I'll ask them if they heard the speaker, and they just look at me blankly, but I know what I'm hearing. It's just so clear, and it keeps happening, and I just don't understand why I'm the only one who can hear them.
Do the voices ever talk about you, perhaps commenting on your actions or discussing you in the third person?

No, no, they don't really do that. It's not about me at all, which is... well, it's part of why I'm so confused by the whole thing. You'd think if a voice was coming through the speaker right where I'm standing, it would be paying attention to what I'm doing, right? Like, "Oh, she's walking to room 402," or "She's checking vitals." But they don't care about my actions whatsoever. I could be emptying a Foley catheter, or changing out some soiled linens, or just sitting at the desk charting my own shift notes, and they never say a single word about me or what I'm doing. 

I've never heard them use my name or talk about me to each other like I'm not there. It's strictly about the hospital. The records. Like I was saying before, it's just this constant, very clinical listing of what's being hidden. Just last Tuesday, I was standing right by the med cart, completely minding my own business, getting some Tylenol ready for a patient, and the voice came through the vent right above the cart. It didn't say, "She's getting the medication." It just went straight into, "Room 410, chart altered. Room 412, labs deleted." 

It's never about me. It feels more like I'm just... I don't know, like I'm just a radio receiver that happens to be tuned into the right frequency to catch a broadcast. They aren't talking to me about me, they're just exposing these secrets, and I'm the only one catching it. Which honestly just makes it all the more frustrating, because why am I the one hearing it if it has absolutely nothing to do with me? I've worked on this same unit for fifteen years, I do my job perfectly, I know every protocol, so why am I the one getting burdened with all this information about the charts?
Do you feel like the voices are part of some larger scheme or that they're trying to involve you in something that others aren't aware of?

Well, yes, exactly! That's exactly it. Because it's not just random babble coming out of those vents, it's a very specific pattern, and it all points to this... this massive cover-up. I mean, I've been doing this for fifteen years, right? I know how the charting is supposed to look. And I know for a fact, I am absolutely certain, that the wound-care charts are showing a pattern that management desperately doesn't want anyone to see. 

I started noticing it a few weeks ago, maybe a month, when the voices first started listing off the room numbers. I went and looked, and sure enough, there were all these discrepancies in the wound measurements and the infection protocols. And when I brought it up to my supervisor—because that's what you do, right? You follow the chain of command, you report anomalies—she just brushed me off! She sat there in her little office and told me, "Oh, it's just late entries, it's just coding mistakes, don't worry about it." 

But I know she was lying. I could see it in her eyes, the way she wouldn't look directly at me when she said it. It's not coding mistakes! You don't get coding mistakes on twelve different patients in the exact same way, all on the same wing. And now, I can tell they're watching me. I can feel it when I'm at the nurses' station. They're watching what I write in my own shift notes, checking to see if I'm documenting what I know. Because I'm the one who caught it, you see? The voices told me where to look, and I looked, and now management knows that I know. They're trying to keep this whole thing under wraps, whatever they're doing with those wound-care patients, and they're terrified because I'm the only one on the floor who isn't blind to it.
Has anything like this ever happened to you before, where you heard voices or noticed patterns that others didn't seem to recognize?

Well, no, not like this. I mean, sure, over fifteen years on the floor you notice things—like when a new doctor is cutting corners or when the pharmacy is habitually late on their rounds—but nothing like these voices coming through the call-lights or the vents. And I certainly never saw these deliberate, hidden messages buried in the wound-care charts before. All of this... it's entirely new. 

It really all started right around the time the hospital announced that massive new electronic health record rollout. It was supposed to streamline everything, but it was just a total disaster from the start. And I just felt this... this incredible, overwhelming drive, you know? Like I was the only one who actually understood how the floor operated and I had to be the one to fix it all. I was so wound up about it. I mean, my mind was just racing constantly, trying to piece together how we were going to survive the transition. 

I was working nonstop, picking up extra shifts, staying late to help the newer nurses figure out the charting because they were just hopelessly lost. And I hardly needed any sleep! I'd go home, maybe close my eyes for two, three hours tops, and then I'd be wide awake, practically buzzing with energy, ready to get right back to the facility because I was so absolutely certain that if I wasn't there, the whole system would just collapse. It was only after that started—after I was barely sleeping and just going, going, going, trying to hold the entire unit together single-handedly—that the voices began. That's when they started telling me about the altered records. Before I got so driven and focused on fixing the rollout, it was just the normal beeps and alarms. Nothing like this.

Can you tell me more about this time when you were working nonstop, barely sleeping, and felt like you had to hold the whole unit together? Did you feel unusually energized, maybe even euphoric, during that time?

Euphoric... I mean, I guess you could use that word, but to me, it honestly just felt like I was finally awake. Like, truly, fully awake for the first time in years. You know how most people just sleepwalk through their shifts? They come in, they do the bare minimum, they complain, and they clock out. But not me, not during this. I felt this... this absolute clarity, this brilliant surge of energy where I just knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that I was meant to fix everything at work. Everything. The schedules, the supply closets, the new charting system—I was the only one who could see how the pieces fit together. It was an incredible feeling, like I was operating on a completely different level than everyone else. 

But... well, the problem with operating on a higher level is that everyone else is still down below, dragging their feet. And that's when the frustration would hit. My husband, for example, he would see me pacing the living room at 3 AM, getting my scrubs ready for a double shift, and he'd try to intervene. He'd stand there in his pajamas and say, "You need to slow down, you're pushing yourself too hard, just come to bed." And I would just snap at him. I mean, completely fly off the handle. I’d yell at him because he just couldn't grasp what was at stake! 

And it wasn't just him at home. It was the other nurses at the hospital, too. The very people I was trying to help! I'd be reorganizing the med room or auditing the floor notes at lightning speed, and one of the other nurses would come up and tell me to take a lunch break, or tell me I was going too fast and making them look bad, and I would just bite their heads off right there at the nurses' station. I couldn't tolerate it. It made me so intensely angry because it felt like they were deliberately blocking something incredibly important. Like I was on the verge of saving the entire unit from total collapse, I was holding it all together with my own two hands, and they were treating it like I was just being a busybody. How could they not see it? How could they try to stop me when I was the only one awake enough to actually fix things?
After that time when you were feeling so energized and driven, did you experience a period where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things that usually matter to you?

Down? No. No, not at all. I mean, why would I feel hopeless? If anything, I am the only one who actually has any hope of fixing this whole mess! I haven't felt down or sad or whatever you want to call it. I simply do not have the time for that kind of thing. You see, when you are dealing with something of this magnitude, something that goes all the way up to the hospital administrators, you can't just sit around moping or losing interest in things. Losing interest? Ha! I am more interested than I have ever been in my entire fifteen years on that floor.

My husband keeps asking me if I want to just sit down and watch a movie with him, or if I want to go out to the garden. Because I used to do those things, sure. I used to like planting tomatoes and sitting on the patio on my days off. But it is not that I have lost interest in them because I am sad, it is just that... well, how can I possibly care about tomatoes when there are patients whose charts are being systematically altered? How could anyone? 

So no, I haven't been lying in bed or feeling hopeless. I am up. I am alert. I am documenting everything. I have this notebook, just a regular spiral-bound notebook I bought at the pharmacy down the street, and I have been filling it with the discrepancies. Every time the voices point out a new room number, I write it down. I track the dates, the shift supervisors, the exact wound measurements. I mean, I am doing the work of three auditors right now, on top of my regular duties as a nursing assistant. So I definitely haven't slowed down or felt down. I am just too crucial to this whole operation right now. If I stop to feel sad, they win. Management wins. And I am absolutely not going to let that happen.
During this time when you felt so driven and energized, did you believe you had special abilities or powers that others didn't have?

Special abilities? Powers? Well, I wouldn't call them *powers*, like something out of a comic book or a science fiction movie. That sounds... that sounds childish, honestly. I'm a fifty-year-old woman, I've been a nursing assistant for fifteen years, I don't believe I can fly or shoot lasers out of my eyes or anything ridiculous like that. But did I have something special? Something unique to me? Yes. Absolutely yes. 

It wasn't magic, it was just... it was like a heightened state of awareness. A supreme level of competence that no one else on the floor possessed. I mean, you have to understand the environment I was in. The unit was in total chaos because of this new electronic system, right? Everyone was floundering. But me? I could look at a patient's chart, just glance at the screen for a few seconds, and I could see the entire trajectory of their care. I could see the mistakes the doctors were going to make before they even made them. I could anticipate the supply shortages in the stockroom down to the exact number of gauze pads we would need by Tuesday afternoon. 

It was like... like my brain was processing information at light speed. I didn't need to read the manuals or attend those useless training seminars they forced everyone else to sit through. I just *knew* how the system worked, how it was flawed, and exactly what needed to be done to override the glitches. And it wasn't just the computers. I could walk into a patient's room and just sense the shift in their vitals before the monitors even registered it. I remember walking past room 412, Mrs. Gable's room, and I didn't even look at her, I just knew, I felt it in my bones that her IV had infiltrated. And I went in, and sure enough, her arm was swollen. The RN hadn't caught it, the charge nurse hadn't caught it, but I did. 

So, powers? No. But an unparalleled, crystal-clear insight that allowed me to see the hidden truths of the hospital that everyone else was completely blind to? Yes. I was the only one who could see the whole picture. The only one. And honestly, it’s a heavy burden to bear, being the only person who truly sees what’s happening, especially when the voices are constantly feeding you more pieces of the puzzle that you have to put together yourself.
Have you ever had a period of time when you felt so good or so hyper that you got things done much more quickly than usual, or when people told you that you were talking too fast or acting strangely?

Hyper? I don't know if I would use the word hyper, because that makes it sound like a child who had too much sugar. But energy? Oh, I have so much energy right now, it is unbelievable. It is like I have actual electricity running straight through my veins. People tell me I'm talking too fast, sure, I get that a lot lately. My husband says it all the time. But I'm not talking too fast, everyone else is just thinking too slowly! 

I mean, I will work a full shift on the floor—and you know how exhausting a long shift is, most of the girls half my age are dragging their feet and complaining by hour eight—but I finish my shift and I feel like I am just getting started. I come home and I don't even take my shoes off. I just dive right in. I have so much energy that I'll immediately start cleaning the entire house. I'll scrub the kitchen counters, I'll mop the floors, and then I get to work on the really important stuff. I pull out my notebook and I start rewriting all my notes from the hospital, making sure every single discrepancy I noticed that day is perfectly documented and legible. I even bring home some of the disorganized supplies from the unit—just tape and gauze and things that were left out in the wrong bins—and I sort them all out into proper kits on the kitchen table to bring back the next day because no one else is going to do it. 

And I can't even sit still while I do it! I'm just pacing. I'll be pacing back and forth across the kitchen linoleum, just walking circles around the island, because my mind is firing on all cylinders and I just cannot stop moving. And my husband, he'll come in looking half-asleep, and he just stands there, practically begging me to sit down. He'll say, "Please, you've been on your feet all day, just sit down, you're making me dizzy." He thinks I'm acting strangely because I don't need to rest like he does. But how can I sit down? How can I possibly stop when I am getting more done in a single night than most people do in an entire month? I don't need to sit, I just need to keep moving and get it all sorted out.

Have you ever had a period of time when your mood was extremely elevated, or you felt like you were on top of the world, where you were doing things very rapidly, not sleeping much, and felt like you didn't need to sleep?

On top of the world? I mean... I wouldn't use a cliché like that, it makes it sound like I just won the lottery or I'm at an amusement park or something. It's not a party. But do I feel elevated? Yes, if by elevated you mean I finally, *finally* feel like my eyes are completely open. It is like I have been sleepwalking through my life, just going through the motions on the floor for fifteen years, and suddenly, I am just... awake. I am truly awake. 

And because I'm awake, I know exactly what I am meant to do. I am meant to fix everything at work. Everything. The whole system is fractured, the charting is a disaster, the patient care is slipping through the cracks, and I am the only one with the absolute clarity to put it all back together. I am the one meant to do it. 

But the problem—the real problem—is the people around me. Because they aren't awake. They are still sleepwalking. And then they have the nerve to try and stop me. My husband will stand there while I'm organizing my notes and tell me I need to slow down and rest, or one of the RNs at the nurses' station will tell me to take a breath and leave the supply closet for the next shift, and I just... I completely snap at them. I do. I snap, and I raise my voice, because how can they be so blind? 

I snap at them like they are standing in the middle of a burning building asking me to sit down for a cup of tea. They are blocking something so incredibly important! It makes me so furious, honestly, because I am trying to save these patients and fix this hospital, and they are just in the way. They are literally standing in the way of progress. So yes, I feel incredibly awake and driven, but I have zero patience for anyone who tries to slow me down when I am doing the most important work of my life.

Have you ever experienced a time when you felt extremely down or depressed for several days or more, to the point where you lost interest in things you usually enjoy or felt hopeless about the future?

Down? Hopeless? No, no, absolutely not. I don't even understand how someone could feel hopeless when there is just so much work to be done. I mean, I see it at the hospital all the time—people moping around, complaining about their shifts, dragging their feet down the hallway like the world is ending just because they have to change a bedpan or chart a few extra vitals. You see it in their eyes, that sort of dull, empty look? I don't have that. I have never had that. 

How could I possibly lose interest in things when everything is so incredibly vital right now? If anything, I am more interested in things than I have ever been in my entire fifty years on this earth. I don't have time to be depressed! I have to fix the supply closets, I have to monitor the IVs, I have to rewrite my notes... there aren't enough hours in the day for me to sit around feeling sad or sorry for myself. 

Sure, I told you I get angry, I get so furious when people like my husband or the charge nurse get in my way, but that is not depression. That is just... that's just the frustration of being the only competent person in the room. Hopeless about the future? Doctor, I am the *only* hope for the future of that unit. If I stop, if I sit down and get depressed, the whole floor collapses. The whole system just falls apart. So no, no depression here. Just absolute, unwavering purpose. I just have to keep moving, you see? I have to keep going because if I don't do it, literally no one else will, and I am certainly not going to sit around crying when I have a hospital to save.
Have you ever had a period of time, lasting at least a week, where you felt this same kind of heightened energy and drive, even before you started hearing the voices through the speakers and vents?

Well, if you want to get technical about the exact timeline of it all, yes, the energy—that absolute drive to fix things—that definitely came first. It didn't all just happen at once. 

See, we had this massive rollout at the facility recently. Management decided to implement all these new procedures, and it was just a complete and utter disaster from day one. Nobody knew what they were doing, the nurses were confused, the supplies were a mess, and I was just getting so incredibly wound up about the whole thing because I could see the whole system failing in real time. So I had to step up. I had to. I was working nonstop, pulling extra hours, staying late, coming in early, because I was absolutely certain that I had to fix everything at the facility myself. If I didn't do it, the patients were going to suffer because of management's incompetence. 

I was barely sleeping at all during that time. I mean, who has time to sleep when the entire unit is falling apart and you're the only one trying to hold the walls up? I was just running on pure purpose. Sleeping less, working more, organizing everything. 

And it was only after that—after I was already in high gear, working nonstop and hardly sleeping—that's when I started noticing the other things. I never heard the call-light voices before that period. Never. The voices coming through the intercoms and the vents, the ones in the call-lights telling me what to do... none of that happened before I got so driven about the rollout. And the hidden messages, too! I didn't see any of the hidden messages in the patient charts until after I was already completely consumed with fixing the floor. 

It was like... it was like I had to reach a certain level of being awake, a certain level of momentum, before I could finally tune in to what was actually going on. So, no, the voices and the messages in the charts didn't come out of nowhere. They only started after I was already working around the clock to save the facility. They came to help me finish the job, you see? Because I was finally listening.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt persistently sad, lost interest in things you usually enjoy, or felt hopeless about the future?

I feel like... didn't we just cover this? I mean, whether you're asking about a few days or two whole weeks, the answer is exactly the same. No. Absolutely not. I have never been sad for two weeks. 

Do you have any idea what would happen if I just checked out and moped around for fourteen days? The facility would be in absolute ruins. I mean, it's already hanging by a thread with the way management handled that rollout I was telling you about. If I took two weeks to just... what did you say, lose interest? If I lost interest in my work, the patients would be the ones paying the price. 

I've been a nursing assistant for a long time, and you see these young girls come in, right out of their little training programs, and they get overwhelmed, they get sad, they sit and cry in the breakroom because a patient yelled at them or they had to work a double shift. I don't do that. I don't have the luxury of losing interest. Every single day, I am there, I am present, I am listening to what needs to be done. 

I really don't understand why you keep asking about me being hopeless or sad. It's like you're not hearing what I'm telling you. I am the one fixing things! I am the one with the energy and the answers! Sadness is for people who don't know what their purpose is, and like I said, I know exactly what mine is. I don't have time to sit on the couch and stare at the wall. So no, not for two weeks, not for two days. I just do not have that problem, doctor. I'm too busy.

Have you ever had a period of time, lasting at least a week, where you felt your mood was significantly elevated or irritable, you had much more energy than usual, needed very little sleep, and were doing many things aimed at reaching specific goals, even if others saw your actions as excessive or unusual?

Yes, exactly! That is exactly what I have been trying to explain to you this whole time. It’s like... it’s like for the first time in my entire life, I am finally awake. Really, truly awake. Most people just sleepwalk through their shifts, but some days lately, I feel this absolute, undeniable clarity that I am meant to fix everything at work. Everything. Not just my assigned patient load, but the entire floor, the whole system. 

I go in, and I can just see all the pieces and how they are supposed to fit together. I see the flaws in the new charting system, I see that the supply rooms are stocked completely wrong—I mean, who puts the sterile gauze on the bottom shelf where it can get contaminated? It's idiocy! So I have to fix it. I have this... this incredible energy pushing me forward, like an electric current, and I just know I have to be the one to correct it all. It’s a mission. I don't need to stop, I don't need to rest, because the work is just so vital.

But then you have these people who just do not understand. They just don't get it at all. My husband, for instance. He’ll come out into the kitchen at three in the morning while I'm color-coding my medical reference binders and he'll tell me I need to come to bed, that I need to 'slow down.' Slow down! Can you even imagine? Or the charge nurse at the facility, she’ll pull me aside in the hallway and tell me I'm overstepping my role, that I'm doing too much and I need to pace myself. 

And I just... I snap at them. I can't help it, I get so unbelievably irritable and I just snap, because it feels like they are deliberately blocking something important. They are literally standing in the way of progress! They look at me like my actions are excessive or strange, but it's not excessive to care! Why would I slow down when I am the only one actually solving the problems? If they would just get out of my way and let me do what I am clearly meant to do, the whole unit would run perfectly. But instead, they just nag and interfere, and yes, I snap. I absolutely snap. Because they are completely blind to what's really going on, and I am the only one who is finally awake.
